The Hidden Lives of Highlighters

By Mira Kellermann
July 14, 2026

Every student knows the fluorescent trail of a good highlighter, yet few have wondered where that glow comes from. The answer involves a dye discovered by accident, a printing crisis, and a Japanese stationer who nearly went bankrupt twice.

The accidental dye

In 1963 a chemist at the Carter's Ink Company was debugging a batch of miscolored ink when he noticed the fluorescent residue glowed under ordinary light. The pigment — later sold as pyranine — became the heart of every highlighter since. Read more in our fluorescence primer.

Modern highlighters use water-based ink with pyranine and a touch of pH indicator, which is why old lines fade from yellow to a sickly green: the dye oxidizes slowly at room temperature.

"A highlighter is a promise you make to your future self." — every study blogger, ever

Caring for your markers

  • Store them horizontally so both felt ends stay saturated.
  • Cap them tightly; the solvent evaporates within weeks.
  • Revive a dried tip with a drop of distilled water.
  1. Shake gently with the cap on.
  2. Uncap and test on scrap paper.
  3. If the line stays pale, add water as above.

Quick chemistry

DyeEmission peakTypical color
Pyranine512 nmYellow-green
Rhodamine 6G566 nmOrange-pink
 
pH 7  ->  bright yellow
pH 10 ->  pale green

Happy highlighting — and if you want the full history, the book is worth your afternoon.
